title: H₂O₂-Induced Oxidative Stress in Human Cells: From Adaptation to Damage
content: Human cells regularly encounter oxidative stress caused by fluctuations in the extra- and intracellular levels of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). Accumulation of excess H₂O₂ (peroxide stress) can be triggered by various endogenous or exogenous factors (e.g., pathological conditions, radiation, xenobiotics, toxins). This review examines peroxide stress in human cells within the context of the adaptive homeostasis theory, updating the existing knowledge on the mechanisms of stress adaptation by focusing on recently published research. According to the adaptation concept, under normal physiological conditions, H₂O₂ concentrations in individual cellular compartments fluctuate within a certain homeostatic range. Deviations beyond this range can lead to adaptive (non-damaging) or destructive (damaging) stress. A moderate increase in H₂O₂ concentration elicits an adaptive response; the cell mobilizes its defense mechanisms, including the enzyme systems that remove H₂O₂. The main factor of cell adaptation is the activity of Nrf2 and FOXO transcription factors, as well as metabolic shifts which enable effective reduction of oxidized peroxidases and other redox-active proteins. Redundancy, functional compensation, and flexibility in the use of reducing equivalents allow cellular antioxidant systems to counter peroxide stress until the oxidative load does not overwhelm the cellular adaptation capacity. Once the cell reaches its adaptive limit, peroxide stress becomes damaging. Cellular peroxidase and reductase capacity is exhausted, leading to the accumulation of hyperoxidized proteins, DNA strand breaks, and membrane damage. This loss of antioxidant capacity may result from oxidative inactivation of redox enzymes, such as peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin reductase, or depletion of compounds that supply reducing equivalents, such as reduced glutathione and NADPH. Identifying the components of antioxidant pathways that exert the greatest control over peroxide removal in human cells under different oxidative conditions is critical for the development of new strategies for antioxidant therapy.
